name: Platelet-rich fibrin matrix (PRFM)

card.summary: A platelet concentrate made from the patient's own blood that forms a fibrin scaffold, used in cosmetic and facial rejuvenation procedures to support skin and tissue healing.
card.aka: Platelet-rich fibrin matrix; Fibrinet PRFM; platelet-rich fibrin (related)
card.note: Cosmetic evidence is mostly small studies; PRFM is an autologous procedure done by clinicians.

quick.overview:
Platelet-rich fibrin matrix is an autologous blood product: blood is drawn from the patient, processed to concentrate platelets in a fibrin scaffold, and returned to the face as a gel-like volumizing and rejuvenating treatment. It is a cousin of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), the better-known facial treatment.

Proponents use it for skin quality, fine lines and soft-tissue fill. Reviews describe growth factors released from platelets as the proposed mechanism, and say stronger studies are needed to define results and best use of each preparation.
quick.how: In general terms, a clinician draws a small blood sample, processes it into a matrix and places it in or under the skin of areas such as the under-eyes or cheeks. Sessions are done in clinics, and the matrix has also been used in dental and orthopedic procedures.
quick.risks: Because the material comes from the patient's own blood, allergic reaction is not the main concern; reported issues with injections in general include bruising, swelling and infection risk from the procedure. Reviews describe cosmetic evidence as thin and recommend careful understanding of differences between preparations.

lead: Platelet-rich fibrin matrix (PRFM) is an autologous platelet concentrate: a small sample of the patient's own blood is processed into a gel-like fibrin scaffold packed with platelets, then placed in or under the skin. In aesthetics it is offered as a way to improve skin quality, soften folds such as the nasolabial lines and add gentle volume under the eyes and cheeks, so the face looks fresher and smoother.[2][8]

PRFM belongs to a family of preparations sorted by a 2020 review into four groups according to leukocyte content and fibrin architecture; pure platelet-rich fibrin, such as Fibrinet PRFM, is listed as its own category beside platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and leukocyte-rich variants.[1] Proponents say the fibrin scaffold keeps growth factors in place and releases them over a longer period than a liquid PRP injection, which is the main reason clinics choose it for facial work.[1][11][12]

Aesthetic research on PRFM is small. A 15-patient pilot on deep nasolabial folds reported a mean 2.12-point improvement on a wrinkle scale that built through 12 weeks,[8] a registered split-face study compared PRFM with saline in 30 people,[10] and a systematic appraisal of PRP in facial rejuvenation mentioned a single PRFM study among its 36 studies.[6] Most published PRFM trials sit in orthopedics, wound care and dentistry.[14][15]

chain: Patient's blood is processed into a platelet-rich fibrin matrix
Matrix is placed in or under facial skin
Growth factors support tissue repair and mild fill
angle.text: Clinics offer PRFM for skin rejuvenation and gentle volume, for example in the nasolabial folds, cheeks and under-eyes. Platelet growth factors held in a fibrin scaffold are the proposed route to firmer, smoother-looking skin, and the same material has been injected into thinning scalp areas in one registered pilot.

paras: Platelet concentrates are autologous products with higher than baseline platelet counts, intended to enhance healing.[1] Platelet-rich fibrin more broadly is prepared by centrifuging blood without an anticoagulant so that a fibrin clot forms; platelets, leukocytes and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF and EGF are held in the clot, and it has been used mainly as a scaffold in oral and maxillofacial surgery.[5]

PRFM as a named product refers to the pure platelet-rich fibrin preparation made with commercial kits, notably the Fibrinet system (originally from Cascade Medical Enterprises). A laboratory description of Fibrinet found a dense, mechanically robust matrix with platelets concentrated on one side, and growth factors including PDGF, EGF, VEGF, bFGF and TGF-beta1 released with levels peaking at day one and declining afterwards.[11] Because the material is activated and clotted into a gel, it differs from liquid PRP, which is injected as a plasma suspension.[1]

Platelet-rich plasma entered surgery in the 1990s and spread through oral surgery, orthopedics and sports medicine before reaching cosmetic practice; a review of PRP in skin and hair describes its use for youthful skin and hair growth.[20] Platelet-rich fibrin as a second-generation concentrate was described in dentistry in the early 2000s, and a 2006 paper on its technological concepts is the standard citation for the method.[5]

PRFM followed through proprietary kit systems. A US trial of Cascade PRFM on rotator cuff healing was registered in 2005,[18] and in 2008 a pilot of 21 patients tested a PRFM membrane on chronic leg ulcers.[15] An early aesthetic pilot on nasolabial folds began in 2008 and was published in 2010 by facial plastic surgeon Anthony Sclafani.[17][8]

Public awareness of platelet treatments in appearance culture came mainly through PRP, marketed as the 'vampire facelift' or 'vampire facial'; PRFM is usually mentioned by clinics as a thicker, longer-lasting alternative for folds and under-eye hollows. In looksmaxxing and skincare communities it is discussed far less than PRP, microneedling or fillers.

Facial rejuvenation uses platelet preparations including PRP and PRFM for skin rejuvenation and tissue fill, and a review notes that different processing methods yield preparations with different components and properties.[2] Practitioners describe placing PRFM intradermally or in the upper subdermis along folds, and with a microcannula in the mid-cheek and nasolabial regions in a registered split-face design.[8][10]

Registered studies by the same New York group also tested the matrix on hair density in frontal and crown alopecia: a 15-person, single-arm, open-label trial of three monthly intradermal sessions reported mean density at six months of 175.1 percent of baseline in 13 completers and no adverse events, without a control group.[9]

Facial aesthetics. In a pilot study of 15 adults, a single injection of activated PRFM into the dermis and upper subdermis beneath deep nasolabial folds produced a mean Wrinkle Assessment Scale reduction of 2.12 with improvement growing at 2, 6 and 12 weeks; the author reported no fibrosis, lumpiness or restricted movement and concluded the matrix may stimulate dermal augmentation.[8] A registered split-face study at New York Medical College (30 participants, started 2018) compared 4 mL of PRFM with saline across the mid-cheek and nasolabial fold using VISIA skin scores at 6 and 12 weeks; no results had been posted to the registry.[10]

Reviews of the field. A systematic appraisal of PRP in facial rejuvenation identified 36 studies and 3,172 patients with a median of 27.5 per study; it reported that a single PRFM study found it relatively safe and effective with greatest benefit at 12 weeks, and the authors described the evidence as very limited and asked for consensus endpoints.[6] A 2014 review of growth factors in skin rejuvenation likewise described one prospective PRFM study alongside in vitro and animal work and small PRP series, calling for larger studies.[13]

Orthopedics. A randomized trial of 60 rotator cuff repair patients reported no significant difference in pain, motion, most functional scores or structural integrity between PRFM and no augmentation at early follow-up.[14] A separate study examined at-risk tears.[19] A randomized study of PRFM in rotator cuff healing is also on record,[4] and a 2018 editorial asked whether PRFM was 'for real', noting that evidence for biologic augments in tendon problems is largely retrospective and small.[7]

Wounds, dentistry and urology. The 2008 ulcer pilot reported closure in about two-thirds of venous ulcer patients within roughly six weeks.[15] Randomized trials in periodontal defects and furcation lesions, and implant stability studies, have used PRFM alone or with bone graft materials or stem cells.[3] A retrospective series of 17 urology patients reported minor injection-site pain and bruising in three men.[16]

Platelet alpha granules contain growth factors that signal cells involved in repair; in the putative mechanism, these factors are the active agents behind a reparative tissue response.[2] In a cell and animal study, PRFM released growth factors slowly, and VEGF from the matrix drove endothelial cell proliferation through the ERK pathway and improved angiogenesis in a delayed ischemic wound model.[12] Researchers describe the fibrin scaffold as holding cells in place and prolonging release compared with a PRP gel.[1]

Because the product is the patient's own blood, allergic reaction to the material is not the main concern; reported effects after injection are bruising, swelling and procedure-related infection risk.[8][16] In 2024 the CDC reported that three women likely acquired HIV from 'vampire facials' at an unlicensed New Mexico spa, the first reported association of HIV transmission with nonsterile cosmetic injection services; investigators found unsafe infection control practices, and the CDC advised confirming that providers are licensed and trained.[21] That investigation concerned PRP facials, but it applies to any blood-drawing procedure done outside clinical standards.

Blood-processing kits for PRP, including the Fibrinet system, were cleared by the FDA as devices for preparing platelet concentrate at the point of care; later submissions cite the Cascade Fibrinet system as a predicate for other PRP devices. Cosmetic use of the resulting preparation is a practitioner's decision.

Closest relatives are PRP facials and PRP hair treatments, microneedling with PRP, and Choukroun-style platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF) used in dentistry.[1] Hyaluronic acid fillers are the usual comparison for fold correction, as the PRFM pilot framed its approach against fillers that provoke fibrous tissue response.[8]

timeline.event: A trial of Cascade PRFM on rotator cuff healing is registered.[18]
Platelet-rich fibrin is described as a second-generation platelet concentrate in dentistry.[5]
Pilot of PRFM membrane in 21 patients with chronic leg ulcers published; a nasolabial fold pilot begins.[15][17]
Sclafani publishes the 15-patient nasolabial fold study; the bifacial Fibrinet matrix is characterised in the laboratory.[8][11]
Laboratory work shows PRFM improves wound angiogenesis through VEGF and ERK signalling.[12]
A single-arm trial of PRFM for hair density begins in New York.[9]
A randomized, double-blinded trial finds no difference in rotator cuff outcomes between PRFM and no augmentation.[14]
An editorial questions evidence for PRFM in orthopedics; a split-face PRFM skin trial starts.[7][10]
A review classifies Fibrinet PRFM as a pure platelet-rich fibrin product.[1]
A systematic appraisal finds 36 facial PRP studies and one PRFM study.[6]
CDC reports HIV transmission linked to vampire facials at an unlicensed spa.[21]

lore.intro: PRFM appears mostly in clinic marketing and clinical literature rather than forum threads; in appearance communities it is usually grouped with PRP facials and other regenerative skin treatments.[2]

claims.claim: PRFM fills deep nasolabial folds using the patient's own tissue.
claims.believers: Clinicians who use it say a single injection can soften folds without a foreign filler, building over weeks.[8]
claims.experts: A 15-patient pilot reported a significant wrinkle-scale reduction at 12 weeks, and a systematic appraisal noted only one PRFM study, calling evidence very limited.[8][6]

claims.claim: The fibrin scaffold gives longer-lasting growth factor release than PRP.
claims.believers: Proponents say the matrix acts as a slow-release depot.[1]
claims.experts: Laboratory work found slow release and growth factor levels peaking at day one in a Fibrinet matrix; whether this changes facial results has not been tested head to head.[11][12]

claims.claim: PRFM can improve skin texture and rejuvenation.
claims.believers: Clinics describe better tone and quality after injections.[2]
claims.experts: A split-face saline-controlled study was completed in 2019 but no results are posted; reviews call for larger studies.[10][13]

claims.believers: The New York pilot reported mean density of 175.1 percent of baseline at six months.[9]
claims.experts: The trial was uncontrolled and had 15 participants, so it cannot separate treatment from other factors.[9]

claims.believers: Orthopedic users suggest biologic augmentation improves repairs.[7]
claims.experts: A double-blinded randomized trial found no significant benefit at early follow-up, and an editorial noted placebo and cost effects.[14][7]

claims.believers: A 2008 pilot reported about two-thirds closure in venous ulcers.[15]
claims.experts: The pilot had 21 patients and no control group; laboratory work supports pro-angiogenic activity.[15][12]
